newsitem.title: USA: Urgent action needed to save Lake Tahoe, Gore told.
newsitem.headline: Urgent action needed to save Lake Tahoe, Gore told.

text.p: Vice President Al Gore held a high-level meeting Friday about Lake Tahoe, one of the nation's scenic treasures, and was told that urgent action was needed to preserve its beauty.

Gore, several Cabinet secretaries, Nevada Gov. Bob Miller and three U.S. senators took part in a three-hour open-air workshop amid the spectactular mountains and forests of the Lake Tahoe basin to discuss serious threats to the region.

The meeting, attended by about 200 people, was a prelude to a visit Saturday by President Clinton. He is expected to announce measures to improve the lake's environment, possibly including new federal funding.

Local planners estimate it will cost $900 million over the next decade to repair some of the damage to the lake, which sits astride the California-Nevada border. The two states have pledged $360 million for the cleanup.

The lake's striking blue colour is threatened by algae, many of the trees around the lake are infested with bark beetles, and the thousands of vehicles carrying tourists to the area have clogged roads and fouled the air.
The lake is a popular tourist spot, attracting skiers in winter and campers, hikers and bicyclists in summer, and fuelling sprawling development in some towns.

Gore and other officials praised a consensus that has developed among local people, including business leaders and environmentalists, that the lake and the forests that draw tourists to the region must be preserved.

"That consensus is based on a realisation that at Lake Tahoe the environment is the economy and the economy is the environment," Gore said, addressing the meeting in a clearing among pine trees against a backdrop of majestic mountains.

"Just as with Yellowstone National Park, the Everglades and the Grand Canyon -- all special places -- we must realise that our economic future and our environmental future are intertwined," Gore said.
Environmentalists warned that Lake Tahoe's waters were losing their former crystal clarity.

"If we take urgent action now, this decline can be reversed. We have a window of opportunity of five to 10 years, after which scientists tell us it will be too late," local environmentalist Trish Ronald told the meeting.

The algae problem has been caused by sediments flowing into the lake carrying phosphorous and nitrogen. The problem has been worsened by erosion and the loss of wetlands that used to filter out pollution.

Gore saw the ailing forest at first hand during an energetic two-mile hike along the Mount Tallac trail above Lake Tahoe. Many of the trees have died from the effect of years of drought and a beetle that is estimated to infest about 15 percent of them.
"The forests are in various stages of distress," said Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman, who oversees the U.S. Forest Service, owner of three-quarters of the forests in the Lake Tahoe basin.
"In addition to removing dead and dying trees, we need to be much more aggressive in reintroducing fire to the basin," he said.
Some officials and environmentalists now say a long-time policy of suppressing fires in national forests is harmful to the forests and increases the danger of huge blazes later.
"Homeowners here in the Tahoe basin understand that a prescribed fire is highly preferable to an out-of-control conflagration," Glickman said.
Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt and U.S. Sens. Dianne Feinstein of California and Harry Reid and Richard Bryan of Nevada also attended the meeting.
Gore announced no specific measures. He said he would brief Clinton Saturday when he arrives to tour the lake and hold a forum about the issue.
